newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban lose two towns, take one. [CORRECTED 15:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban lose two towns, take one. [CORRECTED 15:40 GMT]

text.p: Afghanistan's Islamic Taleban militia lost two strategic towns north of the capital Kabul on Friday but took a northeastern provincial capital, Afghan opposition sources in Pakistan said.

Opposition forces commanded by guerrilla leader Ahmad Shah Masood seized Golbahar, at the mouth of his native Panjsher Valley in Kapisa province, and nearby Jabal os-Siraj in Parwan province, after heavy fighting, a Pakistan-based Afghan news service quoted the sources as saying. Masood's forces were later fighting further south aiming to take the Parwan provincial capital of Charikar, the private Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) reported.
But it said Taleban fighters that had advanced through the strategic Salang Pass earlier this week had captured the Samangan province capital of Aibak on Wednesday night.
It was not immediately clear if the Taleban controlled the whole of Samangan province or only a part. (Corrects province name to Samangan from Baghlan).

AIP said the Taleban, who captured Kabul last September and now control nearly 90 percent of the country, sent reinforcements from the capital to join the retreating fighters from Jabal os-Siraj, about 70 km (43 miles) to the north.
The Taleban's Kapisa province governor, Maulvi Khushal, was killed in the fighting for Golbahar, AIP said.

Masood's fighters began attacking Taleban positions in the area on Thursday after the purist movement was ousted from the newly captured Mazar-i-Sharif by local ethnic Uzbek and Shi'ite Moslem forces.
Witnesses said the Taleban on Friday were in full control of the strategic northeastern town of Pul-i-Khumri, although an anti-Taleban official said the opposition had taken it.

Ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani's ambassador to India, Masood Khalili, said in New Delhi that Pul-i-Khumri in Baghlan province, which the Taleban captured on Wednesday, had been retaken by opposition forces overnight.
Witnesses said there was a large attendance at mosques in Pul-i-Khumri for the traditional Friday congregations.

Khalili told a news conference in New Delhi that opposition forces were firmly in control of the strategic Salang Pass, about 100 km (60 miles) north of Kabul, they had taken Pul-i-Khumri town overnight and were advancing towards Charikar, a main town south of the pass.
There was no immediate independent word about the status of the Salang Pass, which a Taleban force had crossed earlier this week before taking Pul-i-Khumri.
But Afghan sources said this Taleban force seemed to be isolated with surrounding areas being in opposition hands after the fall of Jabal os-Siraj to Masood's fighters.
